newsitem.title: USA: No evidence of racial slurs on Texaco tapes - counsel.
newsitem.headline: No evidence of racial slurs on Texaco tapes - counsel.

text.p: An independent attorney appointed by Texaco Inc. to investigate allegations that former company officials used racist language when discussing a discrimination lawsuit against Texaco said Monday there was no evidence they uttered such slurs.

Attorney Michael Armstrong said an analysis of audio tapes which had purported to show three Texaco executives using racist words had been "seriously innacurate in important respects and that words or parts of words were lost."

The tapes came into the public domain after then-personnel coordinator Richard Lundwall made them available to lawyers representing black employees who alleged they were denied opportunities for promotion at the nation's third largest oil company. Lundwall secretly recorded the conversations.
Shortly after that, in November, Texaco settled the lawsuit out of court for $176 million.
One part of the tape which the plaintiffs had alleged described black employees as "black jelly beans" was taken out of context, Armstrong told a news conference at which the report was released.
"The phrase 'black jelly beans,' taken in context and, in the light of extrinsic evidence, was spoken, but had not been intended as a slur," Armstrong's report said.

The transcript of the tapes presented by Armstrong shows former corporate Treasurer Robert Ulrich saying that he had "heard about that diversity thing, we don't have black jelly beans or green" and Lundwall replying, "That's funny, all the black jelly beans seem to be going to the bottom of the bag".
Armstrong also said the Texaco executives had not attempted deliberately to thwart the class-action lawsuit which had been brought by black employees by preventing disclosure of relevant documents.
Instead, he says Ulrich had guarded against sensitive information about employees becoming known to others in the company and outside.
"Ulrich believes that the lawyers' mindset is to ask for everything, but he was trying to be practical and send them only what he decided they needed," Armstrong said.

Earlier this month, Ulrich, who retired from Texaco, pleaded innocent in White Plains, N.Y., to federal charges that he ordered the destruction of documents in the case. Lundwall was also indicted in the document-destruction case. If convicted, each man faces up to 15 years in prison.
Armstrong also said Monday he did not believe that the culture which generated the controversy extended beyond those named in the tapes.
"We found no evidence at all of anyone other than the people who were openly involved," he said.
White Plains-based Texaco has put into effect policies to increase the amount of work it gives to minority- and woman-owned firms and has committed itself publically to equal opportunity programs.
"What the independent investigation makes clear is that there were violations of Texaco's policies and code of conduct," Texaco Chief Executive Peter Bijur said in response to the report.
Texaco stock dipped 62.5 cents to $110.06 on the New York Stock Exchange.
